followUps:
TCP/IP folds OSI layers 5, 6 and 7 (Session, Presentation, Application) into one Application layer, and layers 1 and 2 (Physical, Data Link) into one Link layer.

That leaves 4: Application, Transport, Internet (OSI 3), Link. Session and presentation jobs such as encoding, compression and encryption are done inside the application or its library (for example TLS).

One example per OSI layer: 1 Ethernet cabling or Wi-Fi radio, 2 Ethernet, ARP, 3 IP, ICMP, 4 TCP, UDP, 5 NetBIOS or RPC sessions, 6 TLS record encoding, JPEG, 7 HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH.

Layers 5 and 6 are fuzzy in real life, so people often just say "application".

TLS sits between Transport and Application: it runs on top of TCP and below HTTP, so it is usually said to be at about OSI layers 5 to 6.

HTTPS is simply HTTP bytes passed through TLS first, then TCP. Port 443 carries that stack.

It does not fit one OSI layer cleanly, which is why the model is a vocabulary, not a rule.

ARP is usually placed at layer 2.5, between Data Link and Network. It maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address, so it needs IP (layer 3) knowledge but is carried directly in an Ethernet frame (EtherType 0x0806), with no IP header.

Example: host asks "who has 192.168.1.1?" as a broadcast, and the gateway replies with its MAC.

code.title: Encapsulation: headers added and removed per layer
code.python:
# Encapsulation: each layer adds its header; decapsulation removes them.
layers = [("TCP header", 20), ("IPv4 header", 20), ("Ethernet header+FCS", 18)]
data = "GET /"
size = len(data)
print("application data:", size, "bytes")
for name, n in layers:          # going down the stack: wrap
    size += n
    print("add", name, "->", size, "bytes")
for name, n in reversed(layers):  # going up the stack: unwrap
    size -= n
    print("remove", name, "->", size, "bytes")
# Cost: O(layers) time, O(1) extra space for the sizes.

followUps:
Overhead is 58 bytes per Ethernet frame: TCP 20 + IPv4 20 + Ethernet header 14 + FCS 4 (without options, VLAN tag or preamble).

Sending 1000 bytes of data gives a 1058-byte frame, about 5.5% overhead. Preamble and inter-frame gap add another 20 bytes on the wire.

The Ethernet (link) header changes at every hop, because the source and destination MAC are rewritten for each link. The IP source and destination stay the same end to end, except for the TTL (which drops by 1) and the checksum that follows from it.

Exception: NAT also rewrites IP addresses and ports.

A collision domain is a group of devices whose transmissions can collide because they share one medium.

On a hub, all ports are one domain, so two simultaneous senders corrupt each other's frames. Each full-duplex switch port is its own domain, so collisions effectively disappear.

An L3 switch is a switch that can also route IP between VLANs, doing the lookup in hardware (ASICs) instead of a CPU.

Example: VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on the same switch talk through its routed interfaces at wire speed. It is common in campus and data-centre cores, and it keeps the L2 features too.

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) turns the next-hop IPv4 address into a MAC address on the local link.

The host broadcasts "who has 10.0.0.1?", the owner replies with its MAC, and the answer is cached for a short time. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery for the same job.

The MAC addresses change at every router; the IP addresses stay the same.

A frame from your PC to a remote server has the PC MAC as source and the gateway MAC as destination on the first link. The router builds a fresh frame with its own MAC and the next hop's MAC. The IP header still says PC to server.

code.title: 5-tuple connection table
code.python:
# A TCP connection is identified by the 5-tuple, so one server port serves many clients.
arrivals = [("1.1.1.1", 50000), ("1.1.1.1", 50001), ("2.2.2.2", 50000), ("1.1.1.1", 50000)]
server = ("10.0.0.5", 443)
conns = set()
for ip, port in arrivals:
    t = f"TCP {ip}:{port} -> {server[0]}:{server[1]}"   # the 5-tuple as a key
    new = t not in conns
    conns.add(t)
    print(t, "new connection" if new else "same connection")
print("connections:", len(conns), "on listening ports: 1")
# Cost: O(1) per lookup with a hash set, O(connections) space.

followUps:
The ephemeral range is the block of high port numbers that the OS picks from for the client side of outgoing connections. IANA suggests 49152 to 65535; Linux defaults to 32768 to 60999 (see ip_local_port_range).

That is about 28,000 usable ports on Linux per (source IP, destination IP, destination port) combination.

Port exhaustion is running out of free ephemeral ports, so new outgoing connections fail with errors such as "cannot assign requested address".

Since the 5-tuple must be unique, one client IP talking to one server IP:port has only about 28,000 slots. Connections in TIME_WAIT hold a port for around 60 seconds, so a burst of 500 new connections per second can use them all up.

Fixes: reuse connections (keep-alive, pools), add source IPs, widen the range.

code.title: Learning switch: learn, forward or flood

followUps:
A VLAN splits one physical switch into several separate layer-2 networks, so a broadcast or flood stays inside its own VLAN.

The switch keeps a MAC table per VLAN and tags frames with an 802.1Q VLAN ID on trunk links. Hosts in VLAN 10 never see VLAN 20 floods; to talk across them you need a router.

MAC flooding is an attack that sends many frames with random fake source MACs to fill the switch's MAC table (often a few thousand entries).

When the table is full, the switch cannot learn new hosts and floods unknown traffic like a hub, so an attacker can sniff it. Defence: port security, which limits MACs per port (for example, 2).

NAT happens at the edge router or firewall, where private addresses leave for the internet.

Example: your PC 192.168.1.20:51000 sends out; the router rewrites the source to its public IP 203.0.113.5:40001 and records it in a table. The reply to 40001 is translated back. Servers and data centres often also have NAT or load balancers.

Typically 3 round trips for HTTPS on a new connection before the first byte of the response: about 1 for TCP, 1 for TLS 1.2 (1 with TLS 1.3 plus), then 1 for the HTTP request and response.

Counting DNS (1 more if not cached): DNS 1 + TCP 1 + TLS 1.3 1 + HTTP 1 = 4 RTT. With 50 ms RTT, that is about 200 ms. HTTP/3 (QUIC) merges transport and TLS, saving one round trip.

MTU is the largest packet one link can carry (1500 bytes for Ethernet); MSS is the largest TCP payload per segment, which is MTU minus the IP and TCP headers.

For MTU 1500: MSS = 1500 - 20 - 20 = 1460 bytes. Each side announces its MSS in the SYN.

Fragmentation splits an IP packet that is bigger than the next link's MTU into smaller pieces, which the receiver reassembles.

Example: a 4000-byte packet over MTU 1500 becomes 3 fragments (1480, 1480, 1040 bytes of data). If any one is lost, the whole packet is lost. So TCP avoids it using MSS and path MTU discovery (the DF bit).

code.title: Header overhead and efficiency by payload size
code.python:
# Header overhead for TCP/IPv4/Ethernet: 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 = 58 bytes per frame.
OVERHEAD = 20 + 20 + 14 + 4
for payload in (1, 100, 1000, 1460):
    frame = max(payload + OVERHEAD, 64)    # Ethernet pads frames to a 64-byte minimum
    print(f"payload {payload:4d} -> frame {frame:4d} bytes, efficiency {100 * payload / frame:.1f}%")
# Cost: O(1) per size; the point is the fixed 58-byte cost per frame.

followUps:
MSS = MTU - 40 = 1500 - 20 (IP) - 20 (TCP) = 1460 bytes of data per segment.

With TCP timestamps (12 option bytes) it is usually 1448. Over IPv6, headers are 40+20, so MSS is 1440.

TSO (TCP Segmentation Offload) lets the OS hand the NIC one big buffer, up to 64 KB, and the NIC cuts it into MSS-sized segments and adds the headers.

Example: 64 KB sent as 45 segments of 1460 bytes cost the CPU one trip through the stack, not 45. This lowers CPU use at high speed. GRO/LRO is the receive-side counterpart.

It depends on the diagram, so count by rule: every switch port (full duplex) is one collision domain, and every router interface or VLAN is one broadcast domain.

Example: one router, two switches with 5 hosts each, one link between the switches. Broadcast domains: 2 (one per router interface). Collision domains: ports in use on the switches, 10 hosts + 2 uplinks + 2 router links = about 14. A hub counts as one for all its ports.

A broadcast storm occurs when a layer-2 loop lets broadcast frames circle forever, and each switch keeps copying them out of all ports.

Frames have no TTL at layer 2, so the count grows exponentially and uses up all bandwidth and CPU in seconds. Spanning Tree Protocol blocks redundant links to prevent loops, and storm control limits broadcast rate.

Ossification means the internet's protocols became hard to change because middleboxes (NATs, firewalls, load balancers) assume the exact behaviour of today's protocols and drop anything else.

Example: a new TCP option or a new IP protocol number is often blocked or stripped, so a good new protocol fails in the field. Encrypting headers (QUIC) hides them from boxes so they cannot depend on them.

A new IP-level protocol number would be dropped by many NATs and firewalls, which only pass TCP and UDP, and it would need OS kernel changes everywhere.

UDP is passed almost everywhere, so QUIC rides on it and is implemented in user space, so apps can update it without waiting for OS upgrades. Its own encrypted headers keep it from ossifying.
